entries.66ff1f83a316a2439398fbe5fc1adf196ae82bff: <div sID="gen28296" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="17" osisID="John.17" sID="John.17"/> <div eID="gen28296" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28297" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen28298" type="x-p"/> This chapter is a prayer, it is the Lord's prayer, the Lord Christ's prayer. There was one Lord's prayer which he taught us to pray, and did not pray himself, for he needed not to pray for the forgiveness of sin; but this was properly and peculiarly his, and suited him only as a Mediator, and is a sample of his intercession, and yet is of use to us both for instruction and encouragement in prayer. Observe, I. The circumstances of the prayer, <reference osisRef="John.17.1">ver. 1</reference>. II. The prayer itself. 1. He prays for himself, <reference osisRef="John.17.1-John.17.5">ver. 1-5</reference>. 2. He prays for those that are his. And in this see, (1.) The general pleas with which he introduces his petitions for them, <reference osisRef="John.17.6-John.17.10">ver. 6-10</reference>. (2.) The particular petitions he puts up for them [1.] That they might be kept, <reference osisRef="John.17.11-John.17.16">ver. 11-16</reference>. [2.] That they might be sanctified, <reference osisRef="John.17.17-John.17.19">ver. 17-19</reference>. [3.] That they might be united, <reference osisRef="John.17.11">ver. 11</reference> and <reference osisRef="John.17.20-John.17.23">20-23</reference>. [4.] That they might be glorified, <reference osisRef="John.17.24-John.17.26">ver. 24-26</reference>.
entries.7378f9a5e2f7bc157a141e4c876eaa4054d2898b: <div eID="gen28298" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen28297" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Christ's Intercessory Prayer.</title> <div sID="gen28299" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> These words spake Jesus, and lifted up his eyes to heaven, and said, Father, the hour is come; glorify thy Son, that thy Son also may glorify thee: <hi type="super">2</hi> As thou hast given him power over all flesh, that he should give eternal life to as many as thou hast given him. <hi type="super">3</hi> And this is life eternal, that they might know thee the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom thou hast sent. <hi type="super">4</hi> I have glorified thee on the earth: I have finished the work which thou gavest me to do. <hi type="super">5</hi> And now, O Father, glorify thou me with thine own self with the glory which I had with thee before the world was. <div eID="gen28299" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28300" type="x-p"/> Here we have, I. The circumstances of this prayer, <reference osisRef="John.17.1">v. 1</reference>. Many a solemn prayer Christ made in the days of his flesh (sometimes he continued all night in prayer), but none of his prayers are recorded so fully as this. Observe, <div eID="gen28300" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28301" type="x-p"/> 1. The time when he prayed this prayer; when he had <hi type="italic">spoken these words,</hi> had given the foregoing farewell to his disciples, he prayed this prayer in their hearing; so that, (1.) It was a prayer after a sermon; when he had spoken from God to them, he turned to speak to God for them. Note, Those we preach to we must pray for. He that was to prophesy upon the dry bones was also to pray, <hi type="italic">Come, O breath, and breathe</hi> upon them. And the word preached should be prayed over, for God <hi type="italic">gives the increase.</hi> (2.) It was a prayer after sacrament; after Christ and his disciples had eaten the passover and the Lord's supper together, and he had given them a suitable exhortation, he closed the solemnity with this prayer, that God would preserve the good impressions of the ordinance upon them. (3.) It was a family-prayer. Christ's disciples were his family, and, to set a good example before the masters of families, he not only, as the son of Abraham, taught his household (<reference osisRef="Gen.18.19">Gen. xviii. 19</reference>), but, as a son of David, blessed his household (<reference osisRef="2Sam.6.20">2 Sam. vi. 20</reference>), prayed for them and with them. (4.) It was a parting prayer. When we and our friends are parting, it is good to part with prayer, <reference osisRef="Acts.20.36">Acts xx. 36</reference>. Christ was parting by death, and that parting should be sanctified and sweetened by prayer. Dying Jacob blessed the twelve patriarchs, dying Moses the twelve tribes, and so, here, dying Jesus the twelve apostles. (5.) It was a prayer that was a preface to his sacrifice, which he was now about to offer on earth, specifying the favours and blessings designed to be purchased by the merit of his death for those that were his; like a deed <hi type="italic">leading the uses of a fine,</hi> and directing to what intents and purposes it shall be levied. Christ prayed then as a priest now offering sacrifice, in the virtue of which all prayers were to be made. (6.) It was a prayer that was a specimen of his intercession, which he ever lives to make for us within the veil. Not that in his exalted state he addresses himself to his Father by way of humble petition, as when he was on earth. No, his intercession in heaven is a presenting of his merit to his Father, with a suing out of the benefit of it for all his chosen ones. <div eID="gen28301" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28302" type="x-p"/> 2. The outward expression of fervent desire which he used in this prayer: He <hi type="italic">lifted up his eyes to heaven,</hi> as before (<reference osisRef="John.11.41">ch. xi. 41</reference>); not that Christ needed thus to engage his own attention, but he was pleased thus to sanctify this gesture to those that use it, and justify it against those that ridicule it. It is significant of the lifting up of the soul to God in prayer, <reference osisRef="Ps.25.1">Ps. xxv. 1</reference>. <hi type="italic">Sursum corda</hi> was anciently used as a call to prayer, <hi type="italic">Up with your hearts,</hi> up to heaven; thither we must direct our desires in prayer, and thence we must expect to receive the good things we pray for. <div eID="gen28302" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28303" type="x-p"/> II. The first part of the prayer itself, in which Christ prays for himself. Observe here, <div eID="gen28303" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28304" type="x-p"/> 1. He prays to God as a Father: He <hi type="italic">lifted up his eyes, and said, Father.</hi> Note, As prayer is to be made to God only, so it is our duty in prayer to eye him as a Father, and to call him <hi type="italic">our Father.</hi> All that have the Spirit of adoption are taught to cry <hi type="italic">Abba, Father,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.17.25">v. 25</reference>. For it will be of great use to us in prayer, both for direction and for encouragement, to call God as we hope to find him. <div eID="gen28304" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28305" type="x-p"/> 2. He prayed for himself first. Though Christ, as God, was prayed to, Christ, as man, prayed; thus <hi type="italic">it became him to fulfill all righteousness.</hi> It was said to him, as it is said to us, <hi type="italic">Ask, and I will give thee,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.2.8">Ps. ii. 8</reference>. What he had purchased he must ask for; and shall we expect to have what we never merited, but have a thousand times forfeited, unless we pray for it? This puts an honour upon prayer, that it was the messenger Christ sent on his errands, the way in which even he corresponded with Heaven. It likewise gives great encouragement to praying people, and cause to hope that even the <hi type="italic">prayer of the destitute</hi> shall not be despised; time was when he that is advocate for us had a cause of his own to solicit, a great cause, on the success of which depended all his honour as Mediator; and this he was to solicit in the same method that is prescribed to us, <hi type="italic">by prayers and supplications</hi> (<reference osisRef="Heb.5.7">Heb. v. 7</reference>), so that he knows the heart of a petitioner (<reference osisRef="Exod.23.9">Exod. xxiii. 9</reference>), he knows the way. Now observe, Christ began with prayer for himself, and afterwards prayed for his disciples; this charity must begin at home, though it must not end there. We must love and pray for our neighbor as ourselves, and therefore must in a right manner love and pray for ourselves first. Christ was much shorter in his prayer for himself than in his prayer for his disciples. Our prayers for the church must not be crowded into a corner of our prayers; in making <hi type="italic">supplication for all saints,</hi> we have room enough to enlarge, and should not straiten ourselves. Now here are two petitions which Christ puts up for himself, and these two are one—that he might be glorified. But this one petition, <hi type="italic">Glorify thou me,</hi> is twice put up, because it has a double reference. To the prosecution of his undertaking further: <hi type="italic">Glorify me, that I may glorify thee,</hi> in doing what is agreed upon to be yet done, <reference osisRef="John.17.1-John.17.3">v. 1-3</reference>. And to the performance of his undertaking hitherto: "<hi type="italic">Glorify me, for I have glorified thee.</hi> I have done my part, and now, Lord, do thine," <reference osisRef="John.17.4-John.17.5">v. 4, 5</reference>. <div eID="gen28305" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28306" type="x-p"/> (1.) Christ here prays to be <hi type="italic">glorified,</hi> in order to his <hi type="italic">glorifying God</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.17.1">v. 1</reference>): <hi type="italic">Glorify thy Son</hi> according to thy promise, <hi type="italic">that thy Son may glorify thee</hi> according to his understanding. Here observe, <div eID="gen28306" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28307" type="x-p"/> [1.] What he prays for—that he might be glorified in this world: "<hi type="italic">The hour is come</hi> when all the powers of darkness will combine to vilify thy Son; now, Father, glorify him." The Father glorified the <hi type="italic">Son</hi> upon earth, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Even in his sufferings, by the signs and wonders which attended them. When they that came to take him were thunder-struck with a word,—when Judas confessed him innocent, and sealed that confession with his own guilty blood,—when the judge's wife asleep, and the judge himself awake, pronounced him righteous,—when the sun was darkened, and the veil of the temple rent, then the Father not only justified, but glorified the Son. Nay, <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Even by his sufferings; when he was crucified, he was magnified, he was glorified, <reference osisRef="John.13.31">ch. xiii. 31</reference>. It was in his cross that he conquered Satan and death; his thorns were a crown, and Pilate in the inscription over his head wrote more than he thought. But, <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> Much more after his sufferings. The Father glorified the Son when he <hi type="italic">raised him from the dead,</hi> showed him openly to chosen witnesses, and poured out the Spirit to support and plead his cause, and to set up his kingdom among men, then he <hi type="italic">glorified him.</hi> This he here prays for, and insists upon. <div eID="gen28307" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28308" type="x-p"/> [2.] What he pleads to enforce this request. <div eID="gen28308" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28309" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> He pleads relation: <hi type="italic">Glorify thy Son;</hi> thy Son as God, as Mediator. It is in consideration of this that the heathen are <hi type="italic">given him for his inheritance;</hi> for <hi type="italic">thou art my Son,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.2.7-Ps.2.8">Ps. ii. 7, 8</reference>. The devil had tempted him to renounce his sonship with an offer of the kingdoms of this world; but he rejected the offer with disdain, and depended upon his Father for his preferment, and here applies himself to him for it. Note, Those that have received the adoption of sons may in faith pray for the inheritance of sons; if sanctified, then glorified: <hi type="italic">Father, glorify thy Son.</hi> <div eID="gen28309" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28310" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> He pleads the time: <hi type="italic">The hour is come;</hi> the season prefixed to an hour. The hour of Christ's passion was determined in the counsel of God. He had often said his hour was not yet come; but now it was come, and he knew it. <hi type="italic">Man knows not his time</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eccl.9.12">Eccl. ix. 12</reference>), but the Son of man did. He calls it <hi type="italic">this hour</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.12.27">ch. xii. 27</reference>), and here, <hi type="italic">the hour;</hi> compare <reference osisRef="Mark.14.35">Mark xiv. 35</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.16.21">ch. xvi. 21</reference>. For the hour of the Redeemer's death, which was also the hour of the Redeemer's birth, was the most signal and remarkable hour, and, without doubt, the most critical, that ever was since the clock of time was first set a going. Never was there such an hour as that, nor did ever any hour challenge such expectations of it before, nor such reflections upon it after. 1. "<hi type="italic">The hour is come</hi> in the midst of which I need to be owned." Now is the hour when this grand affair is come to a crisis; after many a skirmish the decisive battle between heaven and hell is now to be fought, and that great cause in which God's honour and man's happiness are together embarked must now be either won or lost for ever. The two champions David and Goliath, Michael and the dragon, are now entering the lists; the trumpet sounds for an engagement that will be irretrievably fatal either to the one or to the other: "<hi type="italic">Now glorify thy Son,</hi> now give him victory over <hi type="italic">principalities and powers,</hi> now let <hi type="italic">the bruising of his heel</hi> be <hi type="italic">the breaking of the serpent's head,</hi> now let thy Son be so upheld as not to fail nor be discouraged." When Joshua went <hi type="italic">forth conquering and to conquer,</hi> it is said, <hi type="italic">The Lord magnified Joshua;</hi> so he <hi type="italic">glorified his Son</hi> when he made the cross his triumphant chariot. 2. "<hi type="italic">The hour is come</hi> in the close of which I expect to be crowned; <hi type="italic">the hour is come</hi> when I am <hi type="italic">to be glorified,</hi> and, <hi type="italic">set at thy right hand.</hi>" Betwixt him and that glory there intervened a bloody scene of suffering; but, being short, he speaks as if he made little of it: <hi type="italic">The hour is come that I must be glorified;</hi> and he did not expect it till then. Good Christians in a trying hour, particularly a dying hour, may thus plead: "<hi type="italic">Now the hour is come,</hi> stand by me, appear for me, now or never: now <hi type="italic">the earthly tabernacle is to be dissolved, the hour is come that I should be glorified.</hi>" <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.1">2 Cor. v. 1</reference>. <div eID="gen28310" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28311" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> He pleads the Father's own interest and concern herein: <hi type="italic">That thy Son may also glorify thee;</hi> for he had consecrated his whole undertaking to his Father's honour. He desired to be carried triumphantly through his sufferings to his glory, that he might glorify the Father two ways:—1. By <hi type="italic">the death of the cross,</hi> which he was now to suffer. <hi type="italic">Father, glorify thy name,</hi> expressed the great intention of his sufferings, which was to retrieve his Father's injured honour among men, and, by his satisfaction, to come up to the glory of God, which man, by his sin, came short of: "Father, own me in my sufferings, that I may honour thee by them." 2. By the doctrine of the cross, which was now shortly to be published to the world, by which God's kingdom was to be re-established among men. He prays that his Father would so grace his sufferings, and crown them, as not only to take off <hi type="italic">the offence of the cross,</hi> but to make it, <hi type="italic">to those that are saved, the wisdom of God and the power of God.</hi> If God had not glorified Christ crucified, <hi type="italic">by raising him from the dead,</hi> his whole undertaking had been crushed; therefore <hi type="italic">glorify me, that I may glorify thee.</hi> Now thereby he hath taught us, (1.) What to eye and aim at in our prayers, in all our designs and desires—and that is, the honour of God. It being our chief end to glorify God, other things must be sought and attended to in subordination and subserviency to the Lord. "Do this and the other for thy servant, that thy servant may glorify thee. Give me health, that I may glorify thee with my body; success, that I may glorify thee with my estate," &c. <hi type="italic">Hallowed be thy name</hi> must be our first petition, which must fix our end in all our other petitions, <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.11">1 Peter iv. 11</reference>. (2.) He hath taught us what to expect and hope for. If we sincerely set ourselves to glorify our Father, he will not be wanting to do that for us which is requisite to put us into a capacity of glorifying him, to give us the grace he knows sufficient, and the opportunity he sees convenient. But, if we secretly honour ourselves more than him, it is just with him to leave us in the hand of our own counsels, and then, instead of honouring ourselves, we shall shame ourselves. <div eID="gen28311" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28312" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Fourthly,</hi> He pleads his commission (<reference osisRef="John.17.2-John.17.3">v. 2, 3</reference>); he desires to glorify his Father, in conformity to, and in pursuance of, the commission given him: "<hi type="italic">Glorify thy Son, as thou hast given him power, glorify him in the execution of the powers thou hast given him,</hi>" so it is connected with the petition; or, <hi type="italic">that thy Son may glorify thee</hi> according to <hi type="italic">the power given him,</hi> so it is connected with the plea. Now see here the power of the Mediator. <div eID="gen28312" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28313" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">a.</hi> The origin of his power: <hi type="italic">Thou hast given him power;</hi> he has it from God, <hi type="italic">to whom all power belongs.</hi> Man, in his fallen state, must, in order to his recovery, be taken under a new model of government, which could not be erected but by a special commission under the broad seal of heaven, directed to the undertaker of that glorious work, and constituting him sole arbitrator of the grand difference that was, and sole guarantee of the grand alliance that was to be, between God and man; so as to this office, he received his power, which was to be executed in a way distinct from his power and government as Creator. Note, The church's king is no usurper, as the prince of this world is; Christ's right to rule is incontestable. <div eID="gen28313" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28314" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">b.</hi> The extent of his power: He has <hi type="italic">power over all flesh.</hi> (<hi type="italic">a.</hi>) Over all mankind. He has power in and over the world of spirits, the powers of the upper and unseen world are subject to him (<reference osisRef="1Pet.3.22">1 Peter iii. 22</reference>); but, being now mediating between God and man, he here <hi type="italic">pleads his power over all flesh.</hi> They were men whom he was to subdue and save; out of that race he had a remnant given him, and therefore all that rank of beings was <hi type="italic">put under his feet.</hi> (<hi type="italic">b.</hi>) Over mankind considered as corrupt and fallen, for so he is called <hi type="italic">flesh,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.6.3">Gen. vi. 3</reference>. If he had not in this sense been flesh, he had not needed a Redeemer. Over this sinful race the Lord Jesus has all power; and <hi type="italic">all judgment,</hi> concerning them, <hi type="italic">is committed to him;</hi> power to bind or loose, acquit or condemn; <hi type="italic">power on earth to forgive sins</hi> or not. Christ, as Mediator, has the government of the whole world put into his hand; he is king of nations, has power even over those <hi type="italic">that know him not, nor obey his gospel;</hi> whom he does not rule, he over-rules, <reference osisRef="Ps.22.28">Ps. xxii. 28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.72.8">lxxii. 8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.28.18">Matt. xxviii. 18</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.3.35">ch. iii. 35</reference>. <div eID="gen28314" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28315" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">c.</hi> The grand intention and design of this power: <hi type="italic">That he should give eternal life to as many as thou hast given him.</hi> Here is the mystery of our salvation laid open. <div eID="gen28315" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28316" type="x-p"/> (<hi type="italic">a.</hi>) Here is the Father making over the elect to the Redeemer, and giving them to him as his charge and trust; as the crown and recompence of his undertaking. He has a sovereign power over all the fallen race, but a peculiar interest in the chosen remnant; <hi type="italic">all things were put under his feet,</hi> but they were <hi type="italic">delivered into his hand.</hi> <div eID="gen28316" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28317" type="x-p"/> (<hi type="italic">b.</hi>) Here is the Son undertaking to secure the happiness of those that were given him, that he would <hi type="italic">give eternal life to them.</hi> See how great the authority of the Redeemer is. He has lives and crowns to give, eternal lives that never die, immortal crowns that never fade. Now consider how great the Lord Jesus is, who has such preferments in his gift; and how gracious he is in giving eternal life to those whom he undertakes to save. [<hi type="italic">a.</hi>] He sanctifies them in this world, gives them the spiritual life which is eternal life in the bud and embryo, <reference osisRef="John.4.14">ch. iv. 14</reference>. Grace in the soul is heaven in that soul. [<hi type="italic">b.</hi>] He will glorify them in the other world; their happiness shall be completed in the vision and fruition of God. This only is mentioned, because it supposes all the other parts of his undertaking, teaching them, satisfying for them, sanctifying them, and preparing them for that eternal life; and indeed all the other were in order to this; we are <hi type="italic">called to his kingdom and glory,</hi> and <hi type="italic">begotten to the inheritance.</hi> What is last in execution was first in intention, and <hi type="italic">that is eternal life.</hi> <div eID="gen28317" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28318" type="x-p"/> (<hi type="italic">c.</hi>) Here is the subserviency of the Redeemer's universal dominion to this: He has <hi type="italic">power over all flesh,</hi> on purpose that he might give eternal life to the select number. Note, Christ's dominion over the children of men is in order to the salvation of the children of God. <hi type="italic">All things are for their sakes,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.15">2 Cor. iv. 15</reference>. All Christ's laws, ordinances, and promises, which are given to all, are designed effectually to convey spiritual life, and secure eternal life, to all that were given to Christ; he is <hi type="italic">head over all things to the church.</hi> The administration of the kingdoms of providence and grace are put into the same hand, that all things may be made to concur for good to the called. <div eID="gen28318" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28319" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">d.</hi> Here is a further explication of this grand design (<reference osisRef="John.17.3">v. 3</reference>): "<hi type="italic">This is life eternal,</hi> which I am empowered and have undertaken to give, this is the nature of it, and this the way leading to it, <hi type="italic">to know thee the only true God,</hi> and all the discoveries and principles of natural religion, and Jesus Christ whom, thou has sent, as Mediator, and the doctrines and laws of that holy religion which he instituted for the recovery of man out of his lapsed state." Here is, <div eID="gen28319" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28320" type="x-p"/> (<hi type="italic">a.</hi>) The great end which the Christian religion sets before us, and that is, eternal life, the happiness of an immortal soul in the vision and fruition of an eternal God. This he was to reveal to all, and secure to all that were given him. By the gospel <hi type="italic">life and immortality are brought to light,</hi> are brought to hand, a life which transcends this as much in excellency as it does in duration. <div eID="gen28320" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28321" type="x-p"/> (<hi type="italic">b.</hi>) The sure way of attaining this blessed end, which is, by the right knowledge of God and Jesus Christ: "<hi type="italic">This is life eternal, to know thee,</hi>" which may be taken two ways—[<hi type="italic">a.</hi>] <hi type="italic">Life eternal</hi> lies in the knowledge of God and Jesus Christ; the present principle of this life is the believing knowledge of God and Christ; the future perfection of that life will be the intuitive knowledge of God and Christ. Those that are brought into union with Christ, and live a life of communion with God in Christ, know, in some measure, by experience, what eternal life is, and will say, "If this be heaven, heaven is sweet." See <reference osisRef="Ps.17.15">Ps. xvii. 15</reference>. [<hi type="italic">b.</hi>] The knowledge of God and Christ leads to life eternal; this is the way in which Christ gives eternal life, by the knowledge of him that has called us (<reference osisRef="2Pet.1.3">2 Peter i. 3</reference>), and this is the way in which we come to receive it. The Christian religion shows us the way to heaven, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> By directing us to God, as the author and felicity of our being; for Christ died to <hi type="italic">bring us to God.</hi> To know him as our Creator, and to love him, obey him, submit to him, and trust in him, as our owner ruler, and benefactor,—to devote ourselves to him as our sovereign Lord, depend upon him as our chief good, and direct all to his praise as our highest end,—<hi type="italic">this is life eternal.</hi> God is here called the <hi type="italic">only true God,</hi> to distinguish him from the false gods of the heathen, which were counterfeits and pretenders, not from the person of the Son, of whom it is expressly said that he is <hi type="italic">the true God and eternal life</hi> (<reference osisRef="1John.5.20">1 John v. 20</reference>), and who in this text is proposed as the object of the same religious regard with the Father. It is certain there is but one only living and true God and the God we adore is he. He is the true God, and not a mere name or notion; the only true God, and all that ever set up as rivals with him are vanity and a lie; the service of him is the only true religion. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> By directing us to Jesus Christ, as the Mediator between God and man: <hi type="italic">Jesus Christ, whom thou hast sent.</hi> If man had continued innocent, the knowledge of the only true God would have been life eternal to him; but now that he is fallen there must be something more; now that we are under guilt, to know God is to know him as a righteous Judge, whose curse we are under; and nothing is more killing than to know this. We are therefore concerned to know Christ as our Redeemer, by whom alone we can now have access to God; it is life eternal to believe in Christ; and this he has undertaken to give to as many as were given him. See <reference osisRef="John.6.39-John.6.40">ch. vi. 39, 40</reference>. Those that are acquainted with God and Christ are already in the suburbs of life eternal. <div eID="gen28321" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28322" type="x-p"/> (2.) Christ here prays to be glorified in consideration of his having glorified the Father hitherto, <reference osisRef="John.17.4-John.17.5">v. 4, 5</reference>. The meaning of the former petition was, Glorify me in this world; the meaning of the latter is, Glorify me in the other world. <hi type="italic">I have glorified thee on the earth, and now glorify thou me.</hi> Observe here, <div eID="gen28322" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28323" type="x-p"/> [1.] With what comfort Christ reflects on the life he had lived on earth: <hi type="italic">I have glorified thee, and finished my work;</hi> it is as good as finished. He does not complain of the poverty and disgrace he had lived in, what a weary life he had upon earth, as ever any man of sorrows had. He overlooks this, and pleases himself in reviewing the service he had done his Father, and the progress he had made in his understanding. This is here recorded, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> For the honour of Christ, that his life upon earth did in all respects fully answer the end of his coming into the world. Note, 1. Our Lord Jesus had work given him to do by him that sent him; he came not into the world to live at ease, but to go <hi type="italic">about doing good,</hi> and to <hi type="italic">fulfill all righteousness.</hi> His Father gave him his work, his work in the vineyard, both appointed him to it and assisted him in it. 2. <hi type="italic">The work that was given him to do</hi> he finished. Though he had not, as yet, gone through the last part of his undertaking, yet he was so near being <hi type="italic">made perfect through sufferings</hi> that he might say, I have finished it; it was as good as done, he was giving it its finishing stroke <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">eteleiosa</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">I have finished.</hi> The word signifies his performing every part of his undertaking in the most complete and perfect manner. 3. Herein he glorified his Father; he pleased him, he praised him. It is the glory of God that <hi type="italic">his work is perfect,</hi> and the same is the glory of the Redeemer; what he is the author of he will be the finisher of. It was a strange way for the Son to glorify the Father by abasing himself (this looked more likely to disparage him), yet it was contrived that so he should glorify him: "<hi type="italic">I have glorified thee on the earth,</hi> in such a way as men on earth could bear the manifestation of thy glory." <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> It is recorded for example to all, <hi type="italic">that we may follow his example.</hi> 1. We must make it our business to do the work God has appointed us to do, according to our capacity and the sphere of our activity; we must each of us do all the good we can in this world. 2. We must aim at the glory of God in all. We must glorify him on the earth, which he has given <hi type="italic">unto the children of men,</hi> demanding only this quit-rent; on the earth, where we are in a state of probation and preparation for eternity. 3. We must persevere herein to the end of our days; we must not sit down till we have finished our work, and <hi type="italic">accomplished as a hireling our day. Thirdly,</hi> It is recorded for encouragement to all those that rest upon him. If he has <hi type="italic">finished the work that was given him to do,</hi> then he is a complete Saviour, and did not do his work by the halves. And he that finished his work for us will finish it in us <hi type="italic">to the day of Christ.</hi> <div eID="gen28323" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28324" type="x-p"/> [2.] See with what confidence he expects <hi type="italic">the joy set before him</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.17.5">v. 5</reference>): <hi type="italic">Now, O Father, glorify thou me.</hi> It is what he depends upon, and cannot be denied him. <div eID="gen28324" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28325" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> See here what he prayed for: <hi type="italic">Glorify thou me,</hi> as before, <reference osisRef="John.17.1">v. 1</reference>. All repetitions in prayer are not to be counted <hi type="italic">vain repetitions;</hi> Christ <hi type="italic">prayed, saying the same words</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.26.44">Matt. xxvi. 44</reference>), and yet <hi type="italic">prayed more earnestly.</hi> What his Father had promised him, and he was assured of, yet he must pray for; promises are not designed to supersede prayers, but to be the guide of our desires and the ground of our hopes. Christ's being glorified includes all the honours, powers, and joys, of his exalted state. See how it is described. 1. It is a glory with God; not only, <hi type="italic">Glorify my name on earth,</hi> but, <hi type="italic">Glorify me with thine own self.</hi> It was paradise, it was heaven, to be with his Father, as <reference osisRef="Prov.8.30">Prov. viii. 30</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.7.13">Dan. vii. 13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.8.1">Heb. viii. 1</reference>. Note, The brightest glories of the exalted Redeemer were to be displayed within the veil, where the Father manifests his glory. The praises of the upper world are offered up <hi type="italic">to him that sits upon the throne and to the lamb</hi> in conjunction (<reference osisRef="Rev.5.13">Rev. v. 13</reference>), and the prayers of the lower world draw out grace and peace <hi type="italic">from God our Father and our Lord Jesus Christ</hi> in conjunction; and thus the Father has glorified him with himself. 2. It is <hi type="italic">the glory he had with God before the world was.</hi> By this it appears, (1.) That Jesus Christ, as God, had a being <hi type="italic">before the world was,</hi> co-eternal with the Father; our religion acquaints us with one that <hi type="italic">was before all things, and by whom all things consist.</hi> (2.) That his glory with the Father is from everlasting, as well as his existence with the Father; for he was from eternity <hi type="italic">the brightness of his Father's glory,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.1.3">Heb. i. 3</reference>. As God's making the world only declared his glory, but made no real additions to it; so Christ undertook the work of redemption, not because he needed glory, for he had a glory <hi type="italic">with the Father before the world,</hi> but because we needed glory. (3.) That Jesus Christ in his state of humiliation divested himself of this glory, and drew a veil over it; though he was still God, yet he was <hi type="italic">God manifested in the flesh,</hi> not in his glory. He laid down this glory for a time, as a pledge that he would go through with his undertaking, according to the appointment of his Father. (4.) That in his exalted state he resumed this glory, and clad himself again with his former robes of light. Having performed his undertaking, he did, as it were, <hi type="italic">reposcere pignus—take up his pledge,</hi> by this demand, <hi type="italic">Glorify thou me.</hi> He prays that even his human nature might be advanced to the highest honour it was capable of, his body a glorious body; and that the glory of the Godhead might now be manifested in the person of the Mediator, Emmanuel, God-man. He does not pray to be glorified with the princes and great men of the earth: no; he that knew both worlds, and might choose which he would have his preferment in, chose it in the glory of the other world, as far exceeding all the glory of this. He had despised <hi type="italic">the kingdoms of this world and the glory of them,</hi> when Satan offered them to him, and therefore might the more boldly claim the glories of the other world. <hi type="italic">Let the same mind be in us.</hi> "Lord, give the glories of this world to whom thou wilt give them, but let me have my portion of glory in the world to come. It is no matter, though I be vilified with men; but, <hi type="italic">Father, glorify thou me with thine own self.</hi>" <div eID="gen28325" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28326" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> See here what he pleaded: <hi type="italic">I have glorified thee;</hi> and now, in consideration thereof, <hi type="italic">glorify thou me.</hi> For, 1. There was an equity in it, and an admirable becomingness, <hi type="italic">that if God was glorified in him, he should glorify him in himself,</hi> as he had observed, <reference osisRef="John.13.32">ch. xiii. 32</reference>. Such an infinite value there was in what Christ did to glorify his Father that he properly merited all the glories of his exalted state. If the Father was a gainer in his glory by the Son's humiliation, it was fit the Son should be no loser by it at long run, in his glory. 2. It was according to the covenant between them, that if the Son would <hi type="italic">make his soul an offering for sin</hi> he should <hi type="italic">divide the spoil with the strong</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.53.10">Isa. liii. 10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.53.12">12</reference>), and <hi type="italic">the kingdom should be his;</hi> and this he had an eye to, and depended upon, in his sufferings; it was <hi type="italic">for the joy set before him</hi> that <hi type="italic">he endured the cross:</hi> and now in his exalted state he still expects the completing of his exaltation, because he perfected his undertaking, <reference osisRef="Heb.10.13">Heb. x. 13</reference>. 3. It was the most proper evidence of his Father's accepting and approving the work he had finished. By the glorifying of Christ we are satisfied that God was satisfied, and therein a real demonstration was given that the Father was well pleased in him as his beloved Son. 4. Thus we must be taught that those, and only those, who glorify God on earth, and persevere in the work God hath given them to do, shall be glorified with the Father, when they must be no more in this world. Not that we can merit the glory, as Christ did, but our glorifying God is required as an evidence of our interest in Christ, through whom eternal life is God's free gift.
entries.a2edd446df6d0d6c04dfca429faf01fabdc65102: <div eID="gen28326" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Christ's Intercessory Prayer.</title> <div sID="gen28327" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> I have manifested thy name unto the men which thou gavest me out of the world: thine they were, and thou gavest them me; and they have kept thy word. <hi type="super">7</hi> Now they have known that all things whatsoever thou hast given me are of thee. <hi type="super">8</hi> For I have given unto them the words which thou gavest me; and they have received <hi type="italic">them,</hi> and have known surely that I came out from thee, and they have believed that thou didst send me. <hi type="super">9</hi> I pray for them: I pray not for the world, but for them which thou hast given me; for they are thine. <hi type="super">10</hi> And all mine are thine, and thine are mine; and I am glorified in them. <div eID="gen28327" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28328" type="x-p"/> Christ, having prayed for himself, comes next to pray for those that are his, and he knew them by name, though he did not here name them. Now observe here, <div eID="gen28328" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28329" type="x-p"/> I. Whom he did not pray for (<reference osisRef="John.17.9">v. 9</reference>): <hi type="italic">I pray not for the world.</hi> Note, There is a world of people that Jesus Christ did not pray for. It is not meant of the world of mankind general (he prays for that here, <reference osisRef="John.17.21">v. 21</reference>, <hi type="italic">That the world may believe that thou hast sent me</hi>); nor is it meant of the Gentiles, in distinction from the Jews; but the world is here opposed to the elect, who are given to Christ out of the world. Take the world for a heap of unwinnowed corn in the floor, and God loves it, Christ prays for it, and dies for it, <hi type="italic">for a blessing is in it;</hi> but, <hi type="italic">the Lord perfectly knowing those that are his,</hi> he eyes particularly those <hi type="italic">that were given him out of the world,</hi> extracts them; and then take the world for the remaining heap of rejected, worthless chaff, and Christ neither prays for it, nor dies for it, but abandons it, and <hi type="italic">the wind drives it away.</hi> These are called <hi type="italic">the world,</hi> because they are governed by the spirit of this world, and have their portion in it; for these Christ does not pray; not but that there are some things which he intercedes with God for on their behalf, as the dresser for the reprieve of the barren tree; but he does not pray for them in this prayer, that <hi type="italic">have not part nor lot</hi> in the blessings here prayed for. He does not say, I pray against the world, as Elias made intercession against Israel; but, <hi type="italic">I pray not for them,</hi> I pass them by, and leave them to themselves; they are <hi type="italic">not written in the Lamb's book of life,</hi> and therefore not in the breast-plate of the great high-priest. And miserable is the condition of such, as it was of those whom the prophet was forbidden to pray for, and more so, <reference osisRef="Jer.7.16">Jer. vii. 16</reference>. We that know not who are chosen, and who are passed by, must <hi type="italic">pray for all men,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Tim.2.1">1 Tim. ii. 1</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Tim.2.4">4</reference>. While there is life, there is hope, and room for prayer. See <reference osisRef="1Sam.12.23">1 Sam. xii. 23</reference>. <div eID="gen28329" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28330" type="x-p"/> II. Whom he did pray for; not for angels, but for the children of men. 1. He prays <hi type="italic">for those that were given him,</hi> meaning primarily the disciples that had attended <hi type="italic">him in this regeneration;</hi> but it is doubtless to be extended further, to all who come under the same character, who receive and believe the words of Christ, <reference osisRef="John.17.6">v. 6</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.17.8">8</reference>. 2. He prays <hi type="italic">for all that should believe on him</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.17.20">v. 20</reference>), and it is not only the petitions that follow, but those also which went before, that must be construed to extend to all believers, in every place and every age; for he has a concern for them all, and calls <hi type="italic">things that are not as though they were.</hi> <div eID="gen28330" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28331" type="x-p"/> III. What encouragement he had to pray for them, and what are the general pleas with which he introduces his petitions for them, and recommends them to his Father's favour; they are five:— <div eID="gen28331" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28332" type="x-p"/> 1. The charge he had received concerning them: <hi type="italic">Thine they were, and thou gavest them me</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.17.6">v. 6</reference>), and again (<reference osisRef="John.17.9">v. 9</reference>), <hi type="italic">Thou whom thou hast given me.</hi> "Father, those I am now praying for are such as thou hast entrusted me with, and what I have to say for them is in pursuance of the charge I have received concerning them." Now, <div eID="gen28332" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28333" type="x-p"/> (1.) This is meant primarily of the disciples that then were, who were given to Christ as his pupils to be educated by him while he was on earth, and his agents to be employed for him when he went to heaven. They were given him to be the learners of his doctrine, the witnesses of his life and miracles, and the monuments of his grace and favour, in order to their being the publishers of his gospel and the planters of his church. When they left all to follow him, this was the secret spring of that strange resolution: they were given to him, else they had not given themselves to him. Note, The apostleship and ministry, which are Christ's gift to the church, were first the Father's gift to Jesus Christ. As under the law the Levites were given to Aaron (<reference osisRef="Num.3.9">Num. iii. 9</reference>), to him (the <hi type="italic">great high priest of our profession</hi>) the Father gave the apostles first, and ministers in every age, <hi type="italic">to keep his charge, and the charge of the whole congregation, and to do the service of the tabernacle.</hi> See <reference osisRef="Eph.4.8 Eph.4.11">Eph. iv. 8, 11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.68.18">Ps. lxviii. 18</reference>. Christ received this gift for men, that he might give it to men. As this puts a great honour upon the ministry of the gospel, and magnifies that office, which is so much vilified; so it lays a mighty obligation upon the ministers of the gospel to devote themselves entirely to Christ's service, as being <hi type="italic">given to him,</hi> <div eID="gen28333" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28334" type="x-p"/> (2.) But it is designed to extend to all the elect, for they are elsewhere said to be given to Christ (<reference osisRef="John.6.37">ch. vi. 37</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.6.39">39</reference>), and he often laid a stress upon this, that those he was to save were given to him as his charge; to his care they were committed, from his hand they were expected, and concerning them he received commandments. He here shows, <div eID="gen28334" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28335" type="x-p"/> [1.] That the Father had authority to give them: <hi type="italic">Thine they were.</hi> He did not give that which was none of his own, but covenanted that he had a good title. The elect, whom the Father gave to Christ, were his own in three ways:—<hi type="italic">First,</hi> they were creatures, and their lives and beings were derived from him. When they were given to Christ to be <hi type="italic">vessels of honour,</hi> they were <hi type="italic">in his hand, as clay in the hand of the potter,</hi> to be disposed of as God's wisdom saw most for God's glory. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> They were criminals, and their lives and beings were forfeited to him. It was a remnant of fallen mankind that was given to Christ to be redeemed, that might have been made sacrifices to justice when they were pitched upon to be the <hi type="italic">monuments of mercy;</hi> might justly have been <hi type="italic">delivered to the tormentors</hi> when they were delivered to the Saviour. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> They were chosen, and their lives and beings were designed, for him; they were set apart for God, and were consigned to Christ as his agent. This he insists upon again (<reference osisRef="John.17.7">v. 7</reference>): <hi type="italic">All things whatsoever thou hast given me are of thee,</hi> which, though it may take in all that appertained to his office as Mediator, yet seems especially to be meant of those that were given him. "They <hi type="italic">are of thee,</hi> their being is of thee as the God of nature, their well-being is of thee as the God of grace; they <hi type="italic">are all of thee,</hi> and therefore, Father, I bring them all to thee, that they may be all for thee." <div eID="gen28335" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28336" type="x-p"/> [2.] That he did accordingly give them to the Son. <hi type="italic">Thou gavest them to me,</hi> as sheep to the shepherd, to be kept; as patients to the physician, to be cured; children to a tutor, to be educated; thus he will deliver up his charge (<reference osisRef="Heb.2.13">Heb. ii. 13</reference>), <hi type="italic">The children thou hast given me.</hi> They were delivered to Christ, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> That the election of grace might not be frustrated, <hi type="italic">that not one,</hi> no not <hi type="italic">of the little ones, might perish.</hi> That great concern must be lodged in some one good hand, able to give sufficient security, <hi type="italic">that the purpose of God according to election might stand. Secondly,</hi> That the undertaking of Christ might not be fruitless; they were <hi type="italic">given to him as his seed,</hi> in whom he should <hi type="italic">see of the travail of his soul and be satisfied</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.53.10-Isa.53.11">Isa. liii. 10, 11</reference>), and might not <hi type="italic">spend his strength,</hi> and shed his blood, <hi type="italic">for nought, and in vain,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.49.4">Isa. xlix. 4</reference>. We may plead, as Christ does, "Lord, keep my graces, keep my comforts, for <hi type="italic">thine they were, and thou gavest them to me.</hi>" <div eID="gen28336" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28337" type="x-p"/> 2. The care he had taken of them to teach them (<reference osisRef="John.17.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">I have manifested thy name to them. I have given to them the words which thou gavest to me,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.17.8">v. 8</reference>. Observe here, <div eID="gen28337" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28338" type="x-p"/> (1.) The great design of Christ's doctrine, which was to manifest God's name, to declare him (<reference osisRef="John.1.18">ch. i. 18</reference>), to instruct the ignorant, and rectify the mistakes of a dark and foolish world concerning God, that he might be better loved and worshipped. <div eID="gen28338" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28339" type="x-p"/> (2.) His faithful discharge of this undertaking: <hi type="italic">I have</hi> done it. His fidelity appears, [1.] In the truth of the doctrine. It agreed exactly with the instructions he received from his Father. He gave not only the things, but the very <hi type="italic">words, that were given him.</hi> Ministers, in wording their message, must have an eye to <hi type="italic">the words which the Holy Ghost teaches.</hi> [2.] In the tendency of his doctrine, which was to manifest God's name. He did not seek himself, but, in all he did and said, aimed to magnify his Father. Note, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> It is Christ's prerogative to manifest God's name to the souls of the children of men. <hi type="italic">No man knows the Father, but he to whom the Son will reveal him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.11.27">Matt. xi. 27</reference>. He only has acquaintance with the Father, and so is able to open the truth; and he only has access to the spirits of men, and so is able to open the understanding. Ministers may <hi type="italic">publish the name of the Lord</hi> (as Moses, <reference osisRef="Deut.32.3">Deut. xxxii. 3</reference>), but Christ only can manifest that name. By the word of Christ God is revealed to us; by the Spirit of Christ God is revealed in us. Ministers may speak the words of God to us, but Christ can give us his words, can put them in us, as food, as treasure. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Sooner or later, Christ will manifest God's name to all that were given him, and will give them his word, to be the seed of their new birth, the support of their spiritual life, and the earnest of their everlasting bliss. <div eID="gen28339" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28340" type="x-p"/> 3. The good effect of the care he had taken of them, and the pains he had taken with them, (<reference osisRef="John.17.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">They have kept they word</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.17.7">v. 7</reference>), <hi type="italic">they have known that all things are of thee</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.17.8">v. 8</reference>); <hi type="italic">they have received thy words,</hi> and embraced them, have given their assent and consent to them, <hi type="italic">and have known surely that I came out from thee, and have believed that thou didst send me.</hi> Observe here, <div eID="gen28340" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28341" type="x-p"/> (1.) What success the doctrine of Christ had among those <hi type="italic">that were given to him,</hi> in several particulars:— <div eID="gen28341" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28342" type="x-p"/> [1.] "They have received the words which I gave them, as the ground receives the seed, and the earth drinks in the rain." They attended to the words of Christ, apprehended in some measure the meaning of them, and were affected with them: they received the impression of them. The word was to them an <hi type="italic">ingrafted word.</hi> <div eID="gen28342" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28343" type="x-p"/> [2.] "<hi type="italic">They have kept thy word,</hi> have continued in it; they have conformed to it." Christ's commandment is then only kept when it is obeyed. Those that have to teach others the commands of Christ ought to be themselves observant of them. It was requisite that these should <hi type="italic">keep what was committed to them,</hi> for it was to be transmitted by them to every place for every age. <div eID="gen28343" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28344" type="x-p"/> [3.] "They have understood the word, and have been sensible on what ground they went in receiving and keeping it. They have been aware that thou art the original author of that holy religion which I am come to institute, <hi type="italic">that all things whatsoever thou hast given me are of thee.</hi>" All Christ's offices and powers, all the gifts of the Spirit, all his graces and comforts, which God <hi type="italic">gave without measure to him,</hi> were all from God, contrived by his wisdom, appointed by his will, and designed by his grace, for his own glory in man's salvation. Note, It is a great satisfaction to us, in our reliance upon Christ, that he, and all he is and has, all he said and did, all he is doing and will do, are of God, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.30">1 Cor. i. 30</reference>. We may therefore venture our souls upon Christ's mediation, for it has a good bottom. If the righteousness be of God's appointing, we shall be justified; if the grace be of his dispensing, we shall be sanctified. <div eID="gen28344" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28345" type="x-p"/> [4.] They have set their seal to it: <hi type="italic">They have known surely that I came out from God,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.17.8">v. 8</reference>. See here, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> What it is to believe; it is to <hi type="italic">know surely,</hi> to know <hi type="italic">that it is so of a truth.</hi> The disciples were very weak and defective in knowledge; yet Christ, who knew them better than they knew themselves, passes his word for them that they did believe. Note, We may know surely that which we neither do nor can know fully; <hi type="italic">may know the certainty of the things which are not seen,</hi> though we cannot particularly describe the nature of them. <hi type="italic">We walk by faith,</hi> which knows surely, <hi type="italic">not yet by sight,</hi> which knows clearly. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> What it is we are to believe: <hi type="italic">that Jesus Christ came out from God,</hi> as he is the Son of God, in his person <hi type="italic">the image of the invisible God,</hi> and that God did not send him; that in his undertaking he is the ambassador of the eternal king: so that the Christian religion stands upon the same footing, and is of equal authority, with natural religion; and therefore all the doctrines of Christ are to be received as divine truths, all his commands obeyed as divine laws, and all his promises depended upon as divine securities. <div eID="gen28345" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28346" type="x-p"/> (2.) How Jesus Christ here speaks of this: he enlarges upon it, [1.] As pleased with it himself. Though the many instances of his disciples' dulness and weakness had grieved him, yet their constant adherence to him, their gradual improvements, and their great attainments at last, were his joy. Christ is a Master that delights in the proficiency of his scholars. He accepts the sincerity of their faith, and graciously passes by the infirmity of it. See how willing he is to make the best of us, and to say the best of us, thereby encouraging our faith in him, and teaching us charity to one another, [2.] As pleading it with the Father. He is praying for <hi type="italic">those that were given to him;</hi> and he pleads that they had given themselves to him. Note, The due improvement of grace received is a good plea, according to the tenour of the new covenant, for further grace; for so runs the promise. <hi type="italic">To him that hath shall be given.</hi> Those that keep Christ's word, and believe on him, let Christ alone to commend them, and, which is more, to recommend them to his Father. <div eID="gen28346" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28347" type="x-p"/> 4. He pleads the Father's own interest in them (<reference osisRef="John.17.9">v. 9</reference>): <hi type="italic">I pray for them, for they are thine;</hi> and this by virtue of a joint and mutual interest, which he and the Father have in what pertained to each: <hi type="italic">All mine are thine, and thine are mine.</hi> Between the Father and Son there can be no dispute (as there is among the children of men) about <hi type="italic">meum</hi> and <hi type="italic">tuum—mine and thine,</hi> for the matter was settled from eternity; <hi type="italic">all mine are thine, and thine are mine.</hi> Here is, <div eID="gen28347" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28348" type="x-p"/> (1.) The plea particularly urged for his disciples: <hi type="italic">They are thine.</hi> The consigning of the elect to Christ was so far from making them less the Father's that it was in order to making them the more so. Note, [1.] All that receive Christ's word, and believe in him, are taken into covenant-relation to the Father, and are looked upon as his; Christ presents them to him, and they, through Christ, present themselves to him. Christ has <hi type="italic">redeemed us,</hi> not to himself only, but <hi type="italic">to God, by his blood,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.5.9-Rev.5.10">Rev. v. 9, 10</reference>. They are <hi type="italic">first-fruits unto God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.14.4">Rev. xiv. 4</reference>. [2.] This is a good plea in prayer, Christ here pleads it, <hi type="italic">They are thine;</hi> we may plead it for ourselves, <hi type="italic">I am thine, save me;</hi> and for others (as Moses, <reference osisRef="Exod.32.11">Exod. xxxii. 11</reference>), "<hi type="italic">They are thy people. They are thine;</hi> wilt thou not provide for thine own? Wilt thou not secure them, that they may not be run down by the devil and the world? Wilt thou not secure thy interest in them, that they may not depart from thee? <hi type="italic">They are thine,</hi> own them as thine." <div eID="gen28348" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28349" type="x-p"/> (2.) The foundation on which this plea is grounded: <hi type="italic">All mine are thine, and thine are mine.</hi> This bespeaks the Father and Son to be, [1.] One in essence. Every creature must say to God, <hi type="italic">All mine are thine;</hi> but none can say to him, <hi type="italic">All thine are mine,</hi> but he that is the same in substance with him and equal in power and glory. [2.] One in interest; no separate or divided interests between them. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> What the Father has as Creator is delivered over to the Son, to be used and disposed of in subserviency to his great undertaking. <hi type="italic">All things are delivered to him</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.11.27">Matt. xi. 27</reference>); the grant is so general that nothing is excepted but <hi type="italic">he that did put all things under him. Secondly,</hi> What the Son has as Redeemer is designed for the Father, and his kingdom shall shortly be delivered up to him. All the benefits of redemption, purchased by the Son, are intended for the Father's praise, and in his glory all the lines of his undertaking centre: <hi type="italic">All mine are thine.</hi> The Son owns none for his that are not devoted to the service of the Father; nor will any thing be accepted as a piece of service to the Christian religion which clashes with the dictates and laws of natural religion. In a limited sense, every true believer may say, <hi type="italic">All thine are mine;</hi> if God be ours in covenant, all he is and has is so far ours that it shall be engaged for our good; and in an unlimited sense every true believer does say, Lord, <hi type="italic">all mine are thine;</hi> all laid at his feet, to be serviceable to him. And what we have may be comfortably committed to God's care and blessing when it is cheerfully submitted to his government and disposal: "Lord, take care of what I have, for it is <hi type="italic">all thine.</hi>" <div eID="gen28349" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28350" type="x-p"/> 5. He pleads his own concern in them: <hi type="italic">I am glorified in them</hi>—<hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">dedoxasmai</hi></hi>. (1.) <hi type="italic">I have been glorified in them.</hi> What little honour Christ had in this world was among his disciples; he had been glorified by their attendance on him and obedience to him, their preaching and working miracles in his name; and therefore <hi type="italic">I pray for them.</hi> Note, Those shall have an interest in Christ's intercession in and by whom he is glorified. (2.) "<hi type="italic">I am to be glorified in them</hi> when I am gone to heaven; they are to bear up my name." The apostles preached and wrought miracles <hi type="italic">in Christ's name; the Spirit in them glorified Christ</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.16.14">ch. xvi. 14</reference>): "<hi type="italic">I am glorified in them,</hi> and therefore," [1.] "I concern myself for them." What little interest Christ has in this degenerate world lies in his church; and therefore it and all its affairs lie near his heart, within the veil. [2.] "Therefore I commit them to the Father, who has engaged to glorify the Son, and, upon this account, will have a gracious eye to those in whom he is glorified." That in which God and Christ are glorified may, with humble confidence, be committed to God's special care.
entries.adf76d1a8722bdab21bb8b8173ab5b2b4146b90d: <div eID="gen28350" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Christ's Intercessory Prayer.</title> <div sID="gen28351" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">11</hi> And now I am no more in the world, but these are in the world, and I come to thee. Holy Father, keep through thine own name those whom thou hast given me, that they may be one, as we <hi type="italic">are.</hi> <hi type="super">12</hi> While I was with them in the world, I kept them in thy name: those that thou gavest me I have kept, and none of them is lost, but the son of perdition; that the scripture might be fulfilled. <hi type="super">13</hi> And now come I to thee; and these things I speak in the world, that they might have my joy fulfilled in themselves. <hi type="super">14</hi> I have given them thy word; and the world hath hated them, because they are not of the world, even as I am not of the world. <hi type="super">15</hi> I pray not that thou shouldest take them out of the world, but that thou shouldest keep them from the evil. <hi type="super">16</hi> They are not of the world, even as I am not of the world. <div eID="gen28351" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28352" type="x-p"/> After the general pleas with which Christ recommended his disciples to his Father's care follow the particular petitions he puts up for them; and, 1. They all relate to spiritual blessings in heavenly things. He does not pray that they might be rich and great in the world, that they might raise estates and get preferments, but that they might be kept from sin, and furnished for their duty, and brought safely to heaven. Note, The prosperity of the soul is the best prosperity; for what relates to this Christ came to purchase and bestow, and so teaches us to seek, in the first place, both for others and for ourselves. 2. They are such blessings as were suited to their present state and case, and their various exigencies and occasions. Note, Christ's intercession is always pertinent. Our <hi type="italic">advocate with the Father</hi> is acquainted with all the particulars of our wants and burdens, our dangers and difficulties, and knows how to accommodate his intercession to each, as to Peter's peril, which he himself was not aware of (<reference osisRef="Luke.22.32">Luke xxii. 32</reference>), <hi type="italic">I have prayed for thee.</hi> 3. He is large and full in the petitions, orders them before his Father, and <hi type="italic">fills his mouth with arguments,</hi> to teach us fervency and importunity in prayer, to be large in prayer, and dwell upon our errands at the throne of grace, wrestling as Jacob, <hi type="italic">I will not let thee go, except thou bless me.</hi> <div eID="gen28352" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28353" type="x-p"/> Now the first thing Christ prays for, for his disciples, is their preservation, in <reference osisRef="John.17.11-John.17.16">these verses</reference>, in order to which he commits them all to his Father's custody. Keeping supposes danger, and their danger arose <hi type="italic">from the world,</hi> the world wherein they were, <hi type="italic">the evil</hi> of this he begs they might be kept from. Now observe, <div eID="gen28353" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28354" type="x-p"/> I. The request itself: <hi type="italic">Keep them from the world.</hi> There were two ways of their being delivered from the world:— <div eID="gen28354" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28355" type="x-p"/> 1. By taking them out of it; and he does not pray that they might be so delivered: <hi type="italic">I pray not that thou shouldest take them out of the world;</hi> that is, <div eID="gen28355" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28356" type="x-p"/> (1.) "I pray not that they may be speedily removed by death." If the world will be vexatious to them, the readiest way to secure them would be to hasten them out of it to a better world, that will give them better treatment. Send chariots and horses of fire for them, to fetch them to heaven; Job, Elijah, Jonah, Moses, when that occurred which fretted them, prayed that they might be <hi type="italic">taken out of the world;</hi> but Christ would not pray so for his disciples, for two reasons:—[1.] Because he came to conquer, not to countenance, those intemperate heats and passions which make men impatient of life, and importunate for death. It is his will that we should take up our cross, and not outrun it. [2.] Because he had work for them to do in the world; the world, though sick of them (<reference osisRef="Acts.22.22">Acts xxii. 22</reference>), and therefore not worthy of them (<reference osisRef="Heb.11.38">Heb. xi. 38</reference>), yet could ill spare them. In pity therefore to this dark world, Christ would not have these lights removed out of it, but continued in it, especially for the sake of those in the world that were to <hi type="italic">believe in him through their word.</hi> Let not them be taken out of the world when their Master is; they must each in his own order die a martyr, but not till they have finished their testimony. Note, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> The taking of good people out of the world is a thing by no means to be desired, but rather dreaded and laid to heart, <reference osisRef="Isa.57.1">Isa. lvii. 1</reference>. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Though Christ loves his disciples, he does not presently send for them to heaven, as soon as they are effectually called, but leaves them for some time in this world, that they may do good and glorify God upon earth, and be ripened for heaven. Many good people are spared to live, because they can ill be spared to die. <div eID="gen28356" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28357" type="x-p"/> (2.) "I pray not that they may be totally freed and exempted from the troubles of this world, and taken out of the toil and terror of it into some place of ease and safety, there to live undisturbed; this is not the preservation I desire for them." <hi type="italic">Non ut omni molestia liberati otium et delicias colant, sed ut inter media pericula salvi tamen maneant Dei auxilio—Not that, being freed from all trouble, they may bask in luxurious ease, but that by the help of God they may be preserved in a scene of danger;</hi> so Calvin. Not that they may be kept from all conflict with the world, but that they may not be overcome by it; not that, as Jeremiah wished, they might <hi type="italic">leave their people, and go from them</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.9.2">Jer. ix. 2</reference>), but that, like Ezekiel, <hi type="italic">their faces may be strong against the faces of wicked men,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.3.8">Ezek. iii. 8</reference>. It is more the honour of a Christian soldier by faith to <hi type="italic">overcome the world</hi> than by a monastical vow to retreat from it; and more for the honour of Christ to serve him in a city than to serve him in a cell. <div eID="gen28357" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28358" type="x-p"/> 2. Another way is by keeping them from the corruption that is in the world; and he prays they may be thus kept, <reference osisRef="John.17.11">v. 11</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.17.15">15</reference>. Here are three branches of this petition:— <div eID="gen28358" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28359" type="x-p"/> (1.) <hi type="italic">Holy Father, keep those whom thou hast given me.</hi> <div eID="gen28359" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28360" type="x-p"/> [1.] Christ was now leaving them; but let them not think that their defence was departed from them; no, he does here, in their hearing, commit them to the custody of his Father and their Father. Note, It is the unspeakable comfort of all believers that Christ himself has committed them to the care of God. Those cannot but be safe whom the almighty God keeps, and he cannot but keep those whom the Son of his love commits to him, in the virtue of which we may by faith <hi type="italic">commit the keeping of our souls to God,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.19">1 Pet. iv. 19</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.1.12">2 Tim. i. 12</reference>. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> He here puts them under the divine protection, that they may not be run down by the malice of their enemies; that they and all their concerns may be the particular care of the divine Providence: "<hi type="italic">Keep</hi> their lives, till they have done their work; keep their comforts, and let them not be broken in upon by the hardships they meet with; keep up their interest in the world, and let it not sink." To this prayer is owing the wonderful preservation of the gospel ministry and gospel church in the world unto this day; if God had not graciously kept both, and kept up both, they had been extinguished and lost long ago. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> He puts them under the divine tuition, that they may not themselves run away from their duty, nor be led aside by the treachery of their own hearts: "<hi type="italic">Keep them</hi> in their integrity, keep them disciples, keep them close to their duty." We need God's power not only to put us into a state of grace, but to keep us in it. See, <reference osisRef="John.10.28-John.10.29">ch. x. 28, 29</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.15">1 Pet. i. 5</reference>. <div eID="gen28360" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28361" type="x-p"/> [2.] The titles he gives to him he prays to, and them he prays for, enforce the petition. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> He speaks to God as a <hi type="italic">holy Father.</hi> In committing ourselves and others to the divine care, we may take encouragement, 1. From the attribute of his holiness, for this is engaged for the preservation of his holy ones; he hath <hi type="italic">sworn by his holiness,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.89.35">Ps. lxxxix. 35</reference>. If he be a holy God and hate sin, he will make those holy that are his, and keep them from sin, which they also hate and dread as the greatest evil. 2. From this relation of a Father, wherein he stands to us through Christ. If he be a Father, he will take care of his own children, will teach them and keep them; who else should? <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> He speaks of them as those whom the Father had <hi type="italic">given him.</hi> What we receive as our Father's gifts, we may comfortably remit to our Father's care. "Father, keep the graces and comforts thou hast given me; the children thou hast given me; the ministry <hi type="italic">I have received.</hi>" <div eID="gen28361" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28362" type="x-p"/> (2.) <hi type="italic">Keep</hi> them <hi type="italic">through thine own name.</hi> That is, [1.] Keep them for thy name's sake; so some. "Thy name and honour are concerned in their preservation as well as mine, for both will suffer by it if they either revolt or sink." The Old Testament saints often pleaded, for <hi type="italic">thy name's sake;</hi> and those may with comfort plead it that are indeed more concerned for the honour of God's name than for any interest of their own. [2.] Keep them in thy name; so others; the original is so, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">en to onomati</hi></hi>. "Keep them in the knowledge and fear of thy name; keep them in the profession and service of thy name, whatever it cost them. Keep them in the interest of thy name, and let them ever be faithful to this; keep them in thy truths, in thine ordinances, in the way of thy commandments." [3.] Keep them by or through thy name; so others. "Keep them by thine own power, in thine own hand; keep them thyself, undertake for them, let them be thine own immediate care. Keep them by those means of preservation which thou hast thyself appointed, and by which thou hast made thyself known. Keep them by thy word and ordinances; let thy name be their strong tower, thy tabernacle their pavilion." <div eID="gen28362" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28363" type="x-p"/> (3.) <hi type="italic">Keep them from the evil,</hi> or out of the evil. He had taught them to pray daily, <hi type="italic">Deliver us from evil,</hi> and this would encourage them to pray. [1.] "Keep them from the evil one, the devil and all his instruments; that wicked one and all his children. Keep them from Satan as a tempter, that either he may not have leave to sift them, or that their faith may not fail. Keep them from him as a destroyer, that he may not drive them to despair." [2.] "Keep them from the evil thing, that is sin; from every thing that looks like it, or leads to it. Keep them, that they do no evil," <reference osisRef="2Cor.13.7">2 Cor. xiii. 7</reference>. Sin is that evil which, above any other, we should dread and deprecate. [3.] "Keep them from the evil of the world, and of their tribulation in it, so that it may have no sting in it, no malignity;" not that they might be kept from affliction, but kept through it, that the property of their afflictions might be so altered as that there might be no evil in them, nothing to them any harm. <div eID="gen28363" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28364" type="x-p"/> II. The reasons with which he enforces these requests for their preservation, which are five:— <div eID="gen28364" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28365" type="x-p"/> 1. He pleads that hitherto he had kept them (<reference osisRef="John.17.12">v. 12</reference>): "<hi type="italic">While I was with them in the world, I have kept them in thy name,</hi> in the true faith of the gospel and the service of God; those that thou gavest me for my constant attendants I have kept, they are all safe, and none of them missing, none of them revolted nor ruined, <hi type="italic">but the son of perdition;</hi> he is lost, that the scripture might be fulfilled." Observe, <div eID="gen28365" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28366" type="x-p"/> (1.) Christ's faithful discharge of his undertaking concerning his disciples: <hi type="italic">While he was with them, he kept them,</hi> and his care concerning them was not in vain. He kept them in God's name, preserved them from falling into any dangerous errors or sins, from striking in with the Pharisees, who would have <hi type="italic">compassed sea and land to make proselytes</hi> of them; he kept them from deserting him, and returning to the little all they had left for him; he had them still under his eye and care when he sent them to peach; <hi type="italic">went not his heart with them?</hi> Many that followed him awhile took offence at something or other, and went off; but he kept the twelve that they should not go away. He kept them from falling into the hands of persecuting enemies that sought their lives; kept them when he surrendered himself, <reference osisRef="John.18.9">ch. xviii. 9</reference>. <hi type="italic">While he was with them</hi> he kept them in a visible manner by instructions till sounding in their ears, miracles still done before their eyes; when he was gone from them, they must be kept in a more spiritual manner. Sensible comforts and supports are sometimes given and sometimes withheld; but, when they are withdrawn, yet they are not left comfortless. What Christ here says of his immediate followers is true of all the saints while they are here in this world; Christ keeps them <hi type="italic">in God's name.</hi> It is implied, [1.] That they are weak, and cannot keep themselves; their own hands are not sufficient for them. [2.] That they are, in God's account, valuable and worth the keeping; precious in his sight and honourable; his treasure, his jewels. [3.] That their salvation is designed, for to this it is that they are kept, <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.5">1 Pet. i. 5</reference>. As the wicked are reserved for the day of evil, so the righteous are preserved for the day of bliss. [4.] That they are the charge of the Lord Jesus; for as his charge he keeps them, and exposed himself like the good shepherd for the preservation of the sheep. <div eID="gen28366" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28367" type="x-p"/> (2.) The comfortable account he gives of his undertaking: <hi type="italic">None of them is lost.</hi> Note, Jesus Christ will certainly keep all that were given to him, so that none of them shall be totally and finally lost; they may think themselves lost, and may be nearly lost (in imminent peril); but it is the Father's will that he should <hi type="italic">lose none,</hi> and none he will lose (<reference osisRef="John.6.39">ch. vi. 39</reference>); so it will appear when they come all together, and none of them shall be wanting. <div eID="gen28367" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28368" type="x-p"/> (3.) A brand put upon Judas, as none of those whom he had undertaken to keep. He was among those that were given to Christ, but not of them. He speaks of Judas as already lost, for he had abandoned the society of his Master and his fellow-disciples, and abandoned himself to the devil's guidance, and in a little time would <hi type="italic">go to his own place;</hi> he is as good as lost. But the apostasy and ruin of Judas were no reproach at all to his Master, or his family; for, [1.] He was <hi type="italic">the son of perdition,</hi> and therefore not one of those that were given to Christ to be kept. He deserved perdition, and God left him to throw himself headlong into it. He was the <hi type="italic">son of the destroyer,</hi> as Cain, <hi type="italic">who was of that wicked one.</hi> That great enemy whom the Lord <hi type="italic">will consume</hi> is called a <hi type="italic">son of perdition,</hi> because he is a <hi type="italic">man of sin,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Thess.2.3">2 Thess. ii. 3</reference>. It is an awful consideration that one of the apostles proved a son of perdition.
